The fastest request is the one you never send. HTTP caching lets browsers and CDNs reuse responses instead of downloading them again, and a few headers control all of it. Get them right and pages load instantly; get them wrong and users see old versions after every deploy.

Two Questions Every Cache Asks

When a cache has a stored response, it asks:

  1. Is it still fresh? If yes, use it without contacting the server at all.
  2. If it's stale, has it changed? Ask the server. If nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, and the cache reuses its copy.

Freshness saves the whole request. Revalidation saves the download, but still costs a round trip.

Freshness: Cache-Control

The server says how long a response stays fresh:

Cache-Control: max-age=3600

For the next hour, the browser reuses the response without asking. The most useful directives:

Directive Meaning
max-age=N Fresh for N seconds
s-maxage=N Like max-age, but only for shared caches such as CDNs
no-cache Store it, but check with the server before every use
no-store Don't store it at all
private Only the user's browser may store it, not a CDN
public Any cache may store it, even if the request had credentials
immutable Never changes: don't even revalidate when the user reloads
stale-while-revalidate=N After expiry, serve the old copy for N more seconds while refreshing it in the background

The name no-cache misleads many people: it doesn't forbid caching, it forbids using the cache without checking. To forbid storing, use no-store.

Revalidation: ETag and Last-Modified

To make revalidation possible, the server labels each response.

An ETag is an identifier of the content, often a hash:

ETag: "5f2a9c"

When the copy is stale, the browser asks:

GET /api/products
If-None-Match: "5f2a9c"

If the content still has that ETag, the server answers:

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "5f2a9c"

No body is sent, just the headers. Last-Modified works the same way with a date and If-Modified-Since, but it's less precise: it can't tell two changes within the same second apart.

Settings That Work

Versioned Assets

Build tools name files after their content, like app.3f9c2.js. A new version gets a new name, so the old file can be cached forever:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

This is the single biggest caching win for most sites.

HTML Pages

The HTML must point to the newest asset names, so it should always be checked:

Cache-Control: no-cache

With an ETag, an unchanged page costs a quick 304, and a deploy shows up on the next visit.

API Responses

Public data that changes now and then, like a product list, can be cached briefly and refreshed in the background:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

Private or Sensitive Data

A user's account page or bank balance must never be stored by a shared cache, and often not at all:

Cache-Control: private, no-store

CDNs and the Vary Header

A CDN caches one copy per URL for everyone. If the response depends on a request header, say so with Vary, or one user may get another's version:

Vary: Accept-Encoding

Here the CDN keeps a gzip copy and a brotli copy separately. Be careful with Vary: Cookie or Vary: Authorization: since nearly every request differs, the CDN can barely cache anything. Don't cache personalized responses in a CDN at all; mark them private.

Busting the Cache

When a cached file must change before it expires, you have three options:

  1. Change the URL. New name, new cache entry. The best option, and why build tools add hashes.
  2. Purge the CDN. Works for the CDN, but not for copies already in browsers.
  3. Wait. Which is why long max-age values belong only on versioned files.

Common Mistakes

  • Long max-age on HTML. Users keep an old page that points to old assets after a deploy.
  • no-cache when you meant no-store. Sensitive data still gets stored.
  • Caching personalized pages in a CDN. One user's page served to another. Use private.
  • No validators. Without an ETag or Last-Modified, a stale copy must be downloaded again in full.
  • Short cache times on hashed assets. You pay for revalidation on files that can never change.

The Rules in Short

  1. Hashed assets: max-age=31536000, immutable.
  2. HTML: no-cache, with an ETag.
  3. Shared API data: a short max-age with stale-while-revalidate.
  4. Private data: private, or no-store when it's sensitive.
  5. Send an ETag so stale copies can be revalidated with a cheap 304.
